\textbf{(a)} For $x>0$, $\sqrt{x^2-4x}=x\sqrt{1-4/x}$, so
\[\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x\sqrt{1-4/x}}{x(3-12/x)}=\frac{\sqrt{1}}{3}=\boxed{\tfrac13}.\]
\textbf{(b)} As $x\to\pi^-$, $\sin x\to0^+$ (it is positive just to the left of $\pi$), and $\ln u\to-\infty$ as $u\to0^+$:
\[\lim_{x\to\pi^-}\ln(\sin x)=\boxed{-\infty}.\]
\textbf{(c)} Multiply by the conjugate:
\[\frac{t-\sqrt{t+6}}{t-3}\cdot\frac{t+\sqrt{t+6}}{t+\sqrt{t+6}}=\frac{t^2-t-6}{(t-3)(t+\sqrt{t+6})}=\frac{(t-3)(t+2)}{(t-3)(t+\sqrt{t+6})}=\frac{t+2}{t+\sqrt{t+6}}.\]
So the limit is $\dfrac{5}{3+3}=\boxed{\tfrac56}$.
3: $f$ is increasing everywhere, so $f'>0$ everywhere. The graph of $f$ gets vertical at $x=0$, so $f'(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to0$ from both sides, and it flattens out far from 0, so $f'\to0$. The only graph that is positive on both sides with a vertical asymptote at 0 is \boxed{\text{(d)}}. (Graph (b) has a finite peak, which would mean no vertical tangent.)

Let the point of tangency be $P=(a,\,a^2-a)$. The slope there is $y'=2a-1$. The tangent line also passes through $(0,-1)$, so its slope is
\[\frac{(a^2-a)-(-1)}{a-0}=\frac{a^2-a+1}{a}.\]
Set equal: $a^2-a+1=a(2a-1)=2a^2-a\Rightarrow a^2=1\Rightarrow a=\pm1$. $P$ is in the second quadrant, so $a=-1$, $P=(-1,2)$, slope $-3$:
\[\boxed{y=-3x-1}.\]
